principles.name: AGI focus
principles.description: Committed to building safe, beneficial AGI with a large positive impact on humanity; work that does not help with that is out of scope. The current careers page frames this as 'Humanity first' and 'Feel the AGI': take the stakes of AGI, upside and downside, seriously and with rigor.
evidence_signals: Connects motivation and past work to the mission of safe, beneficial AGI
Shows a considered view on AI safety and benefits, not hype
Names a specific safety or deployment question and gives their own position
Cuts work that does not serve the core goal

principles.name: Intense and scrappy
principles.description: Work hard with urgency, including on unglamorous tasks; be unpretentious, do what works, and take good ideas from anywhere. Close to the current operating principles 'Find a way', 'Intense focus' and 'Update quickly': act with agency, start from a hypothesis and change course fast when the evidence says so.
evidence_signals: Describes doing unglamorous work to unblock a result
Ships a simple solution fast and iterates
Ramps up quickly in an unfamiliar domain and produces results
Changed their mind quickly when data contradicted their first plan

principles.name: Scale
principles.description: Believe scale in models, systems, people, processes and ambition is powerful; when in doubt, scale it up. Not named in the current careers values, but interviewers still probe how designs hold up at 100x or 1,000x load.
evidence_signals: Reasons about what breaks at 10x or 100x
Designs systems and processes that grow without rewrites
Shows ambition in the size of problems taken on

principles.name: Make something people love
principles.description: Technology and products should have a transformative positive effect on people's lives. The current careers page calls this 'Ship joy': research and products that change how people live.
evidence_signals: Talks about real users and how the work changed their experience
Uses user feedback or data to decide what to build
Cares about polish and usefulness, not only capability

principles.name: Team spirit
principles.description: Big advances come from collaboration within and across teams; goals stay aligned and nothing is someone else's problem. The official interview guide evaluates collaboration, communication and openness to feedback, and the current values add 'Act with humility': know the limits of your knowledge and stay open to being wrong.
evidence_signals: Picks up a problem outside their remit because it mattered
Works through disagreement with another team to a shared goal
Is open to feedback and communicates clearly
Admits what they do not know instead of bluffing

rounds.name: Recruiter call
rounds.notes: Background, interest in OpenAI and timing. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager screen
rounds.notes: Can be substantive: past projects, failures and complexity. Some candidates report the 30-minute call is already a full behavioral interview.

rounds.name: Technical screen (coding)
rounds.notes: Practical coding on CoderPad, sometimes a take-home or timed test. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical screen (system design)
rounds.notes: System design, sometimes before the final round.

rounds.name: Final: coding
rounds.notes: Practical coding and refactoring. The official guide says engineering interviews look for well-designed solutions, high-quality code, optimal performance and good test coverage. Some loops add a beta agentic-coding round in an existing codebase where AI tools are allowed. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Final: system design
rounds.notes: Designs often relate to LLM products or infrastructure; interviewers push on scale (100x to 1,000x), reliability and justified technology choices.

rounds.name: Final: project deep dive
rounds.notes: Walk through a past project and the candidate's role in depth; some candidates present a short 4-5 slide deck on a system they built.

rounds.name: Final: leadership behavioral
rounds.notes: Ownership, failures, disagreement and mission alignment, with follow-ups on personal contribution.

rounds.name: Final: cross-functional / working style
rounds.interviewer_role: Cross-functional partner (for example legal or product)
rounds.notes: Collaboration, communication, openness to feedback and explaining technical limits to non-engineers.

rounds.name: Recruiter call
rounds.notes: Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager screen
rounds.notes: Deep dive into research, publications or ML engineering work.

rounds.name: Skills assessment
rounds.notes: Timed coding test or structured technical loop, often ML-flavoured coding. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Final: ML coding
rounds.notes: Multi-part ML coding from simple to hard, often in NumPy or PyTorch (for example a distributed all_gather). Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Final: ML debugging
rounds.notes: Find seeded bugs in a model such as a transformer, then extend it (for example add key-value caching). Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Final: ML systems design
rounds.notes: Training and inference systems, evaluation and data pipelines, deploying and monitoring an LLM.

rounds.name: Final: ML depth / research discussion
rounds.notes: Discussion of a paper assigned in advance (idea, method, findings, limits), then the candidate's own research and overlap with the team. Graduate-level ML theory, such as the RLHF objective, is reported as the hardest bar.

rounds.name: Final: mission and working style
rounds.notes: Fit with mission, research culture, safety views and career goals.

rounds.name: Recruiter call
rounds.notes: Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager screen
rounds.notes: Past launches, failures and motivation, plus what the candidate would do for this team's strategy if already in the role.

rounds.name: Product sense
rounds.notes: AI-native product design and goal setting from a vague prompt; scope early. Often two rounds.

rounds.name: Product execution
rounds.notes: Trade-offs such as capability versus cost, launch plans, and a metrics framework with hero, supporting and counter metrics.

rounds.name: Technical / engineering partner
rounds.notes: Working with research and engineering; model quality versus inference cost; may involve reading an LLM paper beforehand.

rounds.name: Stakeholder: safety and responsible deployment
rounds.interviewer_role: Leader from legal, research, finance or trust and safety
rounds.notes: Balancing velocity against safety, safeguards for agents that act for users, bias detection.

rounds.name: Behavioral
rounds.notes: Collaboration, conflict and communication, including go-to-market partners pushing for off-roadmap work.

rounds.name: Recruiter call
rounds.notes: Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Portfolio screen
rounds.notes: Portfolio walkthrough: the problem, the candidate's own decisions and the outcome.

rounds.name: Final: portfolio presentation
rounds.interviewer_role: Panel of about ten designers, PMs and engineers
rounds.notes: Presentation to a group. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Final: one-on-one portfolio deep dive
rounds.notes: Follow-ups on craft, trade-offs and personal contribution.

rounds.name: Final: whiteboard design exercise
rounds.notes: Design an AI-built app; practical concerns such as whether the flow scales, stays responsive and handles model latency.

rounds.name: Final: product critique
rounds.notes: Critique the design choices of a real product.

rounds.name: Recruiter call
rounds.notes: Which opening fits the candidate's experience and level. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Project retrospective / technical deep dive
rounds.notes: Walk through a large program with technical depth, including architecture questions.

rounds.name: Cross-functional collaboration
rounds.notes: Aligning teams that do not report to you and getting decisions made.

rounds.name: Program scenario
rounds.notes: Diagnose a bottleneck or plan a program (for example a model rollout across products) and structure the fix.

rounds.name: Hiring manager / values
rounds.notes: Working style, interest in AI and fit with the team.

rounds.name: Recruiter or hiring manager call
rounds.notes: Data science track. Background and motivation.

rounds.name: Take-home A/B test
rounds.notes: 48-hour take-home analysis submitted as a slide deck, then a one-hour review: deck plus live SQL or Python, including fixing AI-generated code. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Final: experimentation cases
rounds.notes: Usually two cases with mixed metric results; define success and decide whether to launch.

rounds.name: Final: statistics
rounds.notes: Rapid statistics questions, such as p-values and experiment design.

rounds.name: Final: product partner
rounds.notes: Metrics and goal setting for a product area.

rounds.name: Final: leadership
rounds.notes: Ownership, collaboration and mission fit.

question_patterns.pattern: A time the candidate disagreed with a manager or another team and how they reached alignment
A time the candidate's work hurt the business or a launch failed, and what they learned
Explaining a technical or model limitation to a non-technical stakeholder
A time the candidate learned a new domain quickly and delivered results
Why OpenAI, and how the candidate thinks about safe and beneficial AGI
The project the candidate is proudest of and their exact personal contribution
Design a system that serves or builds on LLMs (search, playground, agents) and its trade-offs
Design scheduling, training or inference systems where GPUs are the scarce resource
Explain why a modelling technique works, or diagnose a training or evaluation problem
Design a well-known product or service (chat, webhooks, storage) at large scale
Decide how to ship a model or feature when capability, cost and safety pull in different directions
Set goals and design an experiment for an AI product launch or onboarding flow
A time the candidate's first plan or belief turned out wrong and how fast they changed course
The most difficult launch or program that needed several teams, and how the candidate kept it moving
Discuss a recent ML paper or the candidate's own research: idea, method, results, limits and next experiments
Ship an AI feature or agent quickly while designing safeguards against misuse, harm or bias
Plan or rescue a program that depends on research timelines and many teams
Design or critique an AI product flow that must handle latency, uncertainty and wrong model output
Read mixed A/B test results, define success and decide whether to launch

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager. How did it go?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real disagreement on substance (priority, design, approach). Show you raised it directly with evidence, listened to the reasoning, and either persuaded or committed fully. Describe the outcome and the relationship afterwards. OpenAI looks for openness to feedback and collaboration over ego. Pitfall: a story where you went around your manager.

looking_for: Whether you raise disagreement directly, with evidence
Whether you put collaboration ahead of ego
strong_signals: A real disagreement on substance
Listens to the reasoning, then persuades or commits
Shows the outcome and the relationship afterwards

sample_questions.question: Describe a time your work had a negative effect on the business. What did you do?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Be candid: what happened, the measurable impact, and your part. Focus on the response: fast detection, mitigation, honest communication, and the durable fix. Show you moved with urgency and did unglamorous cleanup. End with what you do differently now. Pitfall: minimizing or blaming.

looking_for: Whether you own mistakes candidly
How fast and thoroughly you respond to damage
strong_signals: Clear about what happened, the impact and your part
Fast detection, mitigation and honest communication
A durable fix and what you do differently now

sample_questions.question: Tell me about collaborating with a team that disagreed with your approach.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain the shared goal, the competing approaches and why each team held its view. Show how you aligned on the overall goal first, used data or a quick experiment to decide, and treated the outcome as joint. Mention how you kept the relationship healthy. 'Nothing is someone else's problem' is the spirit to show.

looking_for: How you work with a team that sees it differently
Whether you use data to settle disagreements
strong_signals: Aligns on the shared goal first
Uses data or a quick experiment to decide
Treats the outcome as joint and keeps the relationship healthy
watch_outs: Treating the other team as an obstacle
Winning the argument at the cost of trust

sample_questions.question: How did you explain a technical limitation to a non-technical stakeholder?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the stakeholder, what they wanted and the limitation. Show you translated it into impact and options (what is possible, at what cost or risk) using plain language and an example, then agreed next steps. For AI roles, explaining model limits honestly (hallucination, evaluation gaps) is a plus. Pitfall: jargon or just saying no.

looking_for: How you translate technical limits into impact and options
Whether you communicate honestly in plain language
strong_signals: Explains the limitation through impact, cost and risk
Uses a concrete example and agrees on next steps
Is honest about model limits where relevant

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you showed leadership.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Leadership need not mean managing: show taking ownership of an unclear problem, rallying others, making decisions, and delivering. Give scope, obstacles, your actions and a measured result. Show intensity and pragmatism. Pitfall: describing a title rather than actions.

looking_for: Whether you lead through ownership, with or without a title
How you rally others to deliver
strong_signals: Takes on an unclear problem and makes decisions
Gives scope, obstacles, actions and a measured result
Shows urgency and pragmatism
watch_outs: Describing a title instead of actions
A story where others did the hard parts

sample_questions.question: Why do you want to work at OpenAI?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Be specific and sincere: what draws you to the mission of safe, beneficial AGI, which OpenAI work you have followed or used, and how your skills fit this team. Show a balanced view of benefits and risks of AI. Mention what you would contribute, not just gain. Pitfall: generic hype or only prestige.

looking_for: Whether your interest in the mission is specific and sincere
How you see both benefits and risks of AI
strong_signals: Names work you have followed or used
Shows a balanced view of AI benefits and risks
Explains what you would contribute, not just gain
watch_outs: Wanting the job mainly for prestige

sample_questions.question: Walk me through your most impactful project and exactly what you personally did.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give context, the goal, your exact contributions versus the team's, key decisions and alternatives, and the result in numbers. Be ready for deep follow-ups on any detail. Show ramp-up speed and pragmatism. Pitfall: vague 'we' with no clear personal ownership.

looking_for: Exactly what you did versus the team
Whether you can go deep on any detail
strong_signals: Separates your contributions from the team's
Explains key decisions and alternatives
Gives results in numbers
watch_outs: A vague 'we' with no clear ownership

sample_questions.question: What is your view on AI safety and alignment, and what do you think is the most important open problem?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Show you have thought about it: name a concrete problem (for example scalable oversight, evaluation of dangerous capabilities, robustness), explain why it matters and what progress could look like, and how your work could help. Be honest about uncertainty. Interviewers want genuine engagement, not a memorized line.

looking_for: Whether you have thought seriously about AI safety
How you reason about an open, uncertain problem
strong_signals: Names a concrete open problem and why it matters
Describes what progress could look like
Honest about uncertainty and how your work could help
watch_outs: A memorized line with no real view

sample_questions.question: How would you build an LLM-powered search system for a company's internal documents?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify sources, scale, permissions and latency. Cover ingestion and chunking, embeddings plus keyword retrieval, access control enforced at retrieval time, re-ranking, prompt construction with citations, and caching. Discuss evaluation (relevance, groundedness), hallucination mitigation, freshness, and cost per query. Strong answers tie design to user trust.

looking_for: How you design retrieval-based LLM search end to end
Whether you build in permissions, evaluation and trust
strong_signals: Clarifies sources, scale, permissions and latency
Covers chunking, hybrid retrieval, re-ranking and citations
Discusses evaluation, hallucination and cost per query
watch_outs: Leaking documents a user should not see
No way to measure answer quality

sample_questions.question: Design a system that schedules GPU jobs across teams using a credit or quota scheme.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define job types (training, inference, eval), priorities and how credits are granted and spent. Cover a queue and scheduler, bin-packing across nodes, preemption and checkpointing, fairness versus utilization, and accounting. Discuss failure handling when nodes die and how users see wait times. Show reasoning about scarce compute at scale.

looking_for: How you design a fair scheduler for scarce compute
Whether you handle credits, preemption and failures
strong_signals: Defines job types and how credits are granted and spent
Covers bin-packing, preemption and checkpointing
Weighs fairness vs utilization and shows users wait times
watch_outs: Ignoring node failures on long jobs
No accounting for how credits are used

sample_questions.question: Design a playground-style product where developers try models through a web UI backed by an API.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Split frontend and API concerns: auth, model selection and parameters, streaming responses, rate limits and quotas, saving and sharing prompts, and usage metering. Discuss latency (streaming tokens), abuse prevention, and how to roll out new models safely. Show user empathy for developers.

looking_for: How you design a developer-facing product and its API
Whether you show empathy for developer users
strong_signals: Separates frontend and API concerns
Covers auth, streaming, quotas and usage metering
Plans abuse prevention and safe rollout of new models
watch_outs: No rate limits or abuse controls

sample_questions.question: Design a team chat application like Slack.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify features (channels, DMs, presence, search) and scale. Cover persistent connections for real-time delivery, message storage partitioned by channel, ordering, fan-out to large channels, offline sync, and search indexing. Discuss trade-offs in consistency and delivery guarantees. Quantify load.

looking_for: How you design a real-time messaging system at scale
Whether you reason about consistency and delivery
strong_signals: Clarifies features and scale, then quantifies load
Covers persistent connections, partitioned storage and fan-out
Discusses ordering, offline sync and search
watch_outs: No plan for very large channels

sample_questions.question: How would you design a system to train a large model across many machines?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover data, tensor and pipeline parallelism and when each helps, communication cost (all-reduce, interconnect), checkpointing and recovery from node failure, data loading throughput, and monitoring loss and hardware health. Discuss trade-offs between memory, speed and complexity. Strong answers reason from bottlenecks with rough numbers.

looking_for: Whether you understand distributed training parallelism
How you reason from bottlenecks
strong_signals: Explains data, tensor and pipeline parallelism and when each helps
Covers communication cost, checkpointing and node failures
Uses rough numbers to find the bottleneck
watch_outs: Naming techniques without saying when to use them
Ignoring failure recovery on long runs

sample_questions.question: Why does layer normalization tend to work better than batch normalization in transformers?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain both: batch norm normalizes across the batch per feature, layer norm across features per example. Layer norm does not depend on batch size or statistics across variable-length sequences, behaves the same in training and inference, and suits autoregressive and small-batch settings. Mention pre-norm versus post-norm and training stability. Be precise and admit uncertainty where it exists.

looking_for: Whether you understand normalization precisely
How you reason about why one method suits transformers
strong_signals: Explains which axis each method normalizes over
Covers batch size, variable length and train vs inference behavior
Admits uncertainty where it exists
watch_outs: Confident claims that are not accurate

sample_questions.question: Your model performs well on the test set but poorly in production. How do you diagnose a train-test distribution mismatch?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Confirm the gap with production samples and labels. Compare input distributions (feature statistics, embeddings), check for leakage or pipeline differences, and slice errors by segment. Remedies: collect representative data, reweighting, domain adaptation, better evals that mirror production, and monitoring for drift. Show a systematic, experiment-driven approach.

looking_for: How you diagnose a production performance gap
Whether your approach is systematic and experiment-driven
strong_signals: Confirms the gap with real production samples
Compares distributions and checks pipeline differences
Proposes remedies plus drift monitoring

sample_questions.question: How would you build an evaluation suite for an AI agent that must hit accuracy and cost targets?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define tasks representative of real use, success criteria and graders (exact checks, model graders with calibration, human review). Track accuracy, cost per task, latency and failure categories. Discuss contamination, variance across runs, and regression gating in CI. Explain how results drive model or prompt changes.

looking_for: How you design evaluations that reflect real use
Whether you track cost and reliability, not just accuracy
strong_signals: Defines representative tasks and graders
Tracks accuracy, cost, latency and failure types
Handles variance across runs and gates regressions in CI
watch_outs: A single accuracy number with no cost view

sample_questions.question: A new model is ten times more capable but ten times more expensive to run. What would you do with it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Frame who benefits most from the extra capability and what they would pay. Options: premium tier, route only hard queries to it, use it to distill cheaper models, or limited access while cost falls. Consider safety review, capacity, and cannibalization. Recommend a path with metrics (value per query, margin, satisfaction).

looking_for: How you match a costly capability to real value
Whether you weigh cost, safety and capacity
strong_signals: Identifies who benefits most and what they would pay
Compares options like routing, premium tiers or distillation
Recommends a path with metrics such as margin per query
watch_outs: Launching to everyone regardless of cost

sample_questions.question: Design an experiment to improve onboarding for new ChatGPT users.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define the goal (early activation and retention) and a measurable activation event. Form a hypothesis from where new users drop off, design variants, pick primary and guardrail metrics, set sample size and duration, and watch novelty effects and segments. Say what result would change your decision.

looking_for: How you design a sound product experiment
Whether you define activation and success clearly
strong_signals: Defines a measurable activation event
Forms a hypothesis from where users drop off
Sets primary and guardrail metrics, sample size and duration

sample_questions.question: How would you measure success for OpenAI as a company?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Tie metrics to the mission and the business: user value (active use, retention, task success), developer adoption, revenue and compute efficiency, plus safety and trust indicators. Explain trade-offs between them and which you would use as north star. Strong answers acknowledge that mission and growth can conflict.

looking_for: How you tie company metrics to mission and business
Whether you see tensions between goals
strong_signals: Covers user value, developer adoption, revenue and efficiency
Includes safety and trust indicators
Picks a north star and explains trade-offs
watch_outs: Ignoring that mission and growth can conflict

sample_questions.question: Set goals for a hypothetical AI assistant device used in shared public spaces.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify users (owners, bystanders), use cases and constraints (privacy, noise, multiple speakers). Define success metrics for usefulness, adoption and trust, with privacy and safety guardrails. Prioritize a launch scope and say how you would learn before scaling.

looking_for: How you set goals for a new product in a sensitive setting
Whether you account for privacy and bystanders
strong_signals: Clarifies users including bystanders, and constraints
Defines metrics for usefulness, adoption and trust
Prioritizes a launch scope and a plan to learn first

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you were wrong about something important at work.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real belief or plan that mattered, say what evidence showed it was wrong and how quickly you noticed. Show you said so openly, changed course, and limited the cost. Close with how you now test assumptions earlier. OpenAI's current values stress humility and updating quickly. Pitfall: a 'mistake' that is really a strength, or one fixed only after others forced it.

looking_for: Whether you admit being wrong openly
How fast you update when evidence changes
strong_signals: A real belief or plan that mattered
Names the evidence and how quickly they acted on it
Changes how they test assumptions afterwards

sample_questions.question: What was your most difficult cross-functional launch, and what made it hard?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name the launch, the teams involved and the real source of difficulty (conflicting goals, unclear ownership, a hard deadline, a safety or legal question). Show what you personally did to align people, unblock decisions and cut scope, and how the launch went in numbers. Reflect on what you would set up earlier next time. Pitfall: listing teams without showing your own actions.

looking_for: How you drive a launch across teams you do not manage
Whether you can name the real source of difficulty
strong_signals: Clear on the teams, the conflict and their own actions
Unblocks decisions and cuts scope when needed
Gives the outcome and a lesson for next time

sample_questions.question: Imagine you already had this product role. What would you focus on for this team, and what are the risks?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Show you studied the team's products and recent announcements. Name the users and the main opportunity, propose two or three priorities with the reasoning and what you would measure, and call out risks (model limits, cost, safety, competition). Say what you would learn first before committing. Pitfall: a generic roadmap that could fit any company.

looking_for: Whether you understand this team's products and users
How you set priorities and name risks
strong_signals: Refers to the team's actual products
Two or three priorities with reasons and metrics
Names model, cost and safety risks and what to learn first

sample_questions.question: How would you improve ChatGPT for enterprise customers?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Segment enterprise users (admins, knowledge workers, developers) and pick one with a clear pain, such as trust in answers, data controls or getting work done in existing tools. Propose a few solutions, choose one with reasons, and define success (weekly active seats, task completion, expansion) with a guardrail on data safety. Pitfall: listing features with no chosen user or metric.

looking_for: How you pick a user segment and a real pain
Whether you define success and guardrails
strong_signals: Segments admins, workers and developers
Chooses one solution with clear reasons
Success metrics plus a data-safety guardrail
watch_outs: A feature list with no chosen user

sample_questions.question: How would you design safeguards for an AI agent that takes actions on a user's behalf, without killing its usefulness?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Classify actions by risk (read-only, reversible, irreversible or costly) and match controls: confirmations for high-risk steps, scoped permissions, spending limits, audit logs and easy undo. Cover misuse and prompt injection, monitoring and red-teaming before launch. Define metrics for both task success and harm, and stage the rollout. Pitfall: either no guardrails or so many confirmations the agent is useless.

looking_for: How you balance safety and usefulness
Whether you tie controls to the risk of each action
strong_signals: Tiers actions by risk and reversibility
Covers permissions, confirmations, logs and undo
Measures task success and harm, with a staged rollout

sample_questions.question: How would you launch a new ChatGPT model, and how would you measure whether the launch succeeded?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define the goal of the launch and who it is for. Plan staged rollout (internal, small percentage, full), safety evaluation and capacity checks. Pick a hero metric (for example task success or retention), supporting metrics and counter metrics (latency, cost, safety incidents). Say what you would do if instrumentation broke: fallback signals and a rollback rule. Pitfall: a launch plan with no rollback.

looking_for: How you plan a staged, safe launch
Whether your metrics include counter metrics
strong_signals: Staged rollout with safety and capacity checks
Hero, supporting and counter metrics
A fallback if instrumentation fails and a rollback rule

sample_questions.question: You are given a transformer implementation that trains badly. How would you find the bugs, and how would you then add key-value caching for inference?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Debug systematically: overfit a tiny batch, check tensor shapes, attention masking (causal mask direction), softmax axis and scaling, positional encoding, layer norm placement and the loss target shift. Compare against a reference on small inputs. For KV caching, store keys and values per layer from earlier tokens and compute attention only for the new token, noting memory growth with sequence length. Pitfall: guessing instead of isolating.

looking_for: Whether you debug ML code systematically
Whether you understand attention well enough to optimize it
strong_signals: Overfits a tiny batch and checks shapes and masks
Names common bugs: mask, softmax axis, target shift
Explains KV caching and its memory cost
watch_outs: Random changes without isolating the bug

sample_questions.question: Explain the RLHF objective. Why is there a KL penalty to the reference model, and what happens if it is too small or too large?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the setup: a reward model trained on human preferences, then policy optimization to maximize expected reward minus a KL term to the supervised reference model. The KL term limits drift, keeps outputs fluent and reduces reward hacking. Too small: the policy exploits reward model errors. Too large: little improvement over the reference. Mention alternatives such as direct preference optimization. Be precise and admit uncertainty.

looking_for: Whether you understand the RLHF objective precisely
How you reason about the role of the KL term
strong_signals: States reward minus KL to a reference policy
Links the KL term to reward hacking and drift
Explains both failure directions
watch_outs: Confusing the reward model with the policy

sample_questions.question: Design a continuous integration system like GitHub Actions.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify scale (repos, jobs per minute) and features (triggers, workflows, logs, secrets). Cover event intake from pushes, a workflow parser, a job queue with priorities, a fleet of isolated runners with autoscaling, artifact and log storage, secret handling and status reporting. Discuss isolation for untrusted code, retries, fairness between tenants and cost. Pitfall: running untrusted code without isolation.

looking_for: How you design a multi-tenant job execution system
Whether you handle isolation and fairness
strong_signals: Covers triggers, queue, runners, logs and secrets
Isolates untrusted code and autoscales runners
Discusses retries, tenant fairness and cost
watch_outs: One shared queue with no fairness

sample_questions.question: How would you run a program to roll out a new model across several products at once?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the products, the deadline and what 'ready' means. Build a plan with clear owners, a shared launch checklist (evals, safety review, capacity, docs, support), dependencies between research, infrastructure and product teams, and staged rollout with go or no-go gates. Name the top risks and mitigations, a communication cadence, and how you would decide to slip or cut scope. Pitfall: a timeline with no owners or gates.

looking_for: How you structure a large cross-team program
Whether you manage risk and decisions explicitly
strong_signals: Owners, checklist and dependencies made explicit
Staged rollout with go or no-go gates
Top risks, mitigations and a cut-scope rule

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time a research or engineering dependency slipped while other teams were waiting on it. What did you do?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the dependency, who was blocked and the cost of delay. Show you found out early, got the real reason from the team, re-planned with options (cut scope, parallel work, a stopgap) and communicated a new date honestly. Give the outcome and what you changed in how you track risk. Pitfall: just escalating or pushing the research team harder.

looking_for: How you handle a slip you do not control
Whether you communicate honestly and offer options
strong_signals: Detects the slip early and learns the real cause
Re-plans with options such as cutting scope
Shares a new date honestly with blocked teams
watch_outs: Hiding the slip until it is too late

sample_questions.question: Design the main flow of an app built around a language model, where responses can take several seconds and are sometimes wrong.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start from the user and the core task. Handle latency with streaming, progress states and the ability to keep working or cancel. Handle uncertainty with clear sources, easy correction or retry, and feedback controls. Plan empty, error and slow states, and say how the flow scales as features grow. Show how you would test it with users. Pitfall: a polished static screen that ignores latency and wrong answers.

looking_for: Whether you design for model latency and errors
How practical and scalable your flow is
strong_signals: Uses streaming and clear progress states
Lets users check sources, correct or retry
Covers empty, error and slow states
watch_outs: Treating model output as always correct

sample_questions.question: An A/B test shows higher engagement but lower retention in one segment. Define success and decide whether to launch.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Restate the goal and the primary metric chosen before the test. Check validity: sample ratio, duration, novelty effects and multiple comparisons. Break down the segment result and ask whether it is real and how large. Weigh the trade-off against guardrails, then recommend: launch, launch with a fix for the segment, or rerun. Say what extra data would change the decision. Pitfall: picking the metric after seeing results.

looking_for: Whether you check validity before interpreting
How you decide with mixed metrics
strong_signals: Anchors on the pre-chosen primary metric
Checks sample ratio, novelty and multiple tests
Makes a clear launch call with conditions
watch_outs: Choosing the metric after the fact

sample_questions.question: Explain a p-value to a product manager, then describe how you would design a factorial experiment.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define the p-value correctly: the chance of a result at least this extreme if there were no real effect, not the chance the hypothesis is true. Mention significance level, power and practical significance. For a factorial design, test two or more factors together, assign users to every combination, estimate main effects and interactions, and size the sample for the interaction you care about. Pitfall: the common wrong definition.

looking_for: Whether you define a p-value correctly and simply
Whether you understand factorial designs
strong_signals: Correct definition in plain words
Mentions power and practical significance
Explains main effects, interactions and sample size
watch_outs: Saying it is the chance the hypothesis is true

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Early-career engineer delivering scoped work on a team. Public title is Member of Technical Staff.
Independent engineer who owns features or components end to end.
Senior engineer who leads significant projects and sets direction within a team.
Leads technical direction across teams or a major system.

persona.tone: Intense, curious and pragmatic; conversational but high-bar, focused on the candidate's own area of expertise
persona.pace: Fast; follows up quickly and drills into details of the candidate's own work, often starting from a long, open prompt the candidate must clarify
persona.pushback_style: Asks 'what exactly did you do?', 'what breaks at 100x?', 'how would you know it works?' and 'what is your own view on safe deployment?'; stretches the candidate beyond their comfort zone and watches how they take feedback
persona.closing_style: Leaves a few minutes for the candidate's questions about the team and mission

case_style.notes: PM cases are AI-native: product sense from vague prompts (improve ChatGPT for a segment, take a new invention to market, goals for a new device), execution with hero, supporting and counter metrics, launch plans for new models, capability versus cost, and safety versus velocity with legal or trust and safety leaders. No public report mentions classic market-size estimation.

sources.title: OpenAI has quietly changed its core values (Semafor)
OpenAI quietly updates its core values to emphasize AGI development
How to get and ace interviews at OpenAI (Harvard Mignone Center)
OpenAI technical program manager interview guide (CleverPrep)

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: the five principle names are the October 2023 list (Semafor) and are kept as stable ids. As of 2026 the careers page lists different values (Humanity first, Act with humility, Feel the AGI, Ship joy) and operating principles (Find a way, Creativity over control, Update quickly, Intense focus), seen via search snippets of openai.com/careers and two 2026 prep guides; openai.com returned 403 to our fetcher. Descriptions now map the current wording onto the old ids; 'Scale' has no current counterpart, so its weight was lowered to 1.0. A reviewer should decide whether a future version should adopt the new names.

loop_structure: OpenAI's interview guide (403 to our fetcher, read only via search snippets and guides quoting it) confirms an intro call, a team-specific skills assessment, and 4-6 hours of finals with 4-6 people over 1-2 days; round names and durations come from prep guides and vary by team. The design, tpm and other (data science) loops each rest on one or two prep-site write-ups; the tpm loop comes from CleverPrep only.

bar_by_level: still low. OpenAI publishes no levels, and job postings on the Ashby board describe scope by team, not by level (the board did not render for our fetcher; postings were seen via aggregators). Level names L2-L7 appear only on Levels.fyi, which we could not re-check (empty page); scope text is our generic mapping. One guide maps OpenAI L5 to roughly Google or Meta L6, and several report downleveling at offer time. PM, design and TPM levels are not public.

persona: medium because the official guide (via snippets) says finals focus on the candidate's area of expertise, are designed to stretch them beyond their comfort zone, and assess openness to feedback; tone and pushback phrases still come from candidate reports.

scoring_weights: medium; weights are our estimate but derived from the evaluation signals the official guide publishes (well-designed solutions, high-quality code, performance and test coverage; communication, collaboration, openness to feedback and mission alignment; high potential shown by fast ramp-up), cross-checked with 2026 prep guides. No source gives numeric weights.

case_style: medium; three 2026 write-ups (Aced, Aakash Gupta, SupaCV) agree on product sense, execution metrics and safety-versus-velocity cases and none mentions market-size estimation. All are candidate-reported, not official.
